reference_title: Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces asphalt stabilization: treating a subsurface soil/aggregate layer or drainage layer with asphalt cement, typically used where good base course material is unavailable and the subgrade is a sand or silt meeting stabilization requirements, or where a drainage layer will be trafficked by construction equipment; detailed design/construction guidance is in UFC 3-250-11.
sections.body: This chapter contains information for use of asphalt cement for stabilization of soil/aggregate materials and on stabilization of drainage layers. When any subsurface layer receives an asphalt treatment, the treatment is considered asphalt stabilization. In general, asphalt stabilization is utilized where good base course materials are not readily available and where the existing subgrade materials are sands or silts which meet design requirements for stabilization. Asphalt stabilization is used when a drainage layer is trafficked with construction equipment. UFC 3-250-11 contains detailed information on the design and construction of asphalt stabilized soils.
key_points: Any subsurface layer receiving an asphalt treatment is considered asphalt-stabilized.
Used where good base course material is unavailable and the subgrade sand/silt meets stabilization requirements.
Also used to stabilize a drainage layer that will be trafficked by construction equipment.
UFC 3-250-11 is the detailed design/construction reference for asphalt-stabilized soils.
sections.applicability: Applies when a subgrade or drainage layer needs asphalt stabilization instead of, or in addition to, imported base course.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Introduces the two material considerations for asphalt stabilization: the soil/aggregate being treated, covered by suitability criteria in Section 5-2.1, and the asphalt binder used to treat it, covered by emulsion/cutback grade selection in Section 5-2.2.
key_points: Materials for asphalt stabilization are the soil/aggregate being treated and the asphalt binder used to treat it.
See 5-2.1 for soil/aggregate suitability and 5-2.2 for asphalt type selection.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or evaluating the soil/aggregate and asphalt materials for a stabilization project.

sections.title: Soil/Aggregate
sections.summary: Describes soil suitability for asphalt stabilization: governed chiefly by plasticity characteristics and the amount passing the 75 micrometer (No. 200) sieve for fine-grained soils; high-plasticity soils are unsuitable for asphalt stabilization unless pretreated with lime or cement to lower plasticity.
sections.body: There are a number of requirements for determining soil suitability for asphalt stabilization. The stabilization of fine-grained soils depends on the plasticity characteristics and amount of material passing the 75 micrometer (No. 200) sieve. Recommended gradations of materials for various types of asphalt stabilization are given in UFC 3-250-11. Soils with high plasticity are not stabilized with asphalt because of difficulty in thoroughly mixing the asphalt into the soil. These soils are only stabilized if pretreated with lime or cement to decrease the plasticity of the soil.
key_points: Fine-grained soil stabilization suitability depends on plasticity and percent passing the No. 200 (75 micrometer) sieve.
Recommended stabilization gradations are given in UFC 3-250-11.
High-plasticity soils resist thorough asphalt mixing and are excluded unless pretreated with lime or cement to lower plasticity.
sections.applicability: Applies when screening a candidate soil/aggregate for asphalt stabilization suitability.

sections.title: Asphalt
sections.summary: Covers asphalt binder selection for stabilization: emulsified or cutback asphalt is used (slow-set or medium-set emulsions; rapid-set emulsions are not used; any cutback cure rate from rapid to slow is acceptable), with the emulsion-versus-cutback choice driven by material availability, soil type, climate, and construction practice.
sections.body: The asphalt used for stabilization is either emulsified or cutback asphalt. Normally, the emulsions used are slow setting (SS) or possibly some medium setting (MS) emulsions. Rapid set (RS) emulsions are not used. Any type of cutback from rapid (RC) to medium (MC) to slow (SC) cure is used for asphalt stabilization. The use of emulsions versus cutbacks is dependent on the availability of materials, soil type, climate, and construction practice. The availability of cutbacks is limited in areas due to environmental concerns.
key_points: Stabilization asphalt is emulsified (SS or MS grade; RS not used) or cutback (RC/MC/SC cure rates all acceptable).
Emulsion vs. cutback choice depends on material availability, soil type, climate, and construction practice.
Cutback availability is regionally limited due to environmental/emissions concerns.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the binder type/grade for a soil stabilization mix.

sections.title: Composition and Mixture
sections.summary: Notes that the type of asphalt used in stabilized material is as important as the quantity, with UFC 3-250-11 providing guidance on type/amount of liquid asphalt and design procedures for optimum asphalt content for both cutback and emulsified asphalts.
sections.body: For stabilized materials, the type of asphalt used is as important as how much is used. UFC 3-250-11 contains information on the type and amount of liquid asphalt to use. Design procedures for determining optimum asphalt content are given for both cutback and emulsified asphalts.
key_points: Asphalt type matters as much as asphalt quantity in stabilized materials.
UFC 3-250-11 gives type/amount guidance and optimum-asphalt-content design procedures for both cutback and emulsified asphalts.
sections.applicability: Applies when proportioning a stabilized soil/aggregate mixture.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Points to UFC 3-250-11 for the methods and procedures used to construct asphalt-stabilized materials.
sections.body: Methods and procedures for constructing asphalt-stabilized materials are given in UFC 3-250-11.
key_points: Construction methods/procedures for asphalt-stabilized materials are detailed in UFC 3-250-11, not repeated here.
This UFC's role for stabilization construction is to point to the dedicated companion document.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning or inspecting the construction of an asphalt-stabilized layer.

sections.title: Drainage Layers
sections.summary: Introduces asphalt-stabilized drainage layers: subsurface drainage feature design/construction guidance is in FAA AC 150/5320-5E, and open graded material (OGM) is the drainage feature that typically needs stabilization for construction stability or to serve as a structural base for a flexible pavement.
sections.body: Guidance for the design and construction of subsurface drainage features is given in FAA Advisory Circular 150/5320-5E, Airport Drainage Design. Open graded material (OGM) is the drainage feature that normally requires stabilization for construction stability or for structural strength to serve as a base for a flexible pavement.
key_points: FAA AC 150/5320-5E (Airport Drainage Design) is the design/construction reference for subsurface drainage features.
Open graded material (OGM) is the drainage feature that typically needs asphalt stabilization.
Stabilization of OGM serves either construction stability or structural strength as a pavement base.
sections.applicability: Applies to subsurface drainage layers (OGM) that need asphalt stabilization for stability or structural base function.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Gives Marshall-scale asphalt-content guidance for stabilizing open graded material: enough asphalt to coat and hold the aggregate without filling voids, typically about 2 to 2.5 percent by weight of total mixture, with more open gradations needing less asphalt and higher-viscosity asphalt providing greater stability.
sections.body: Ensure the amount of asphalt used coats the aggregate and holds it in place but does not fill any voids. Normally 2 to 2.5 percent (by weight of total mixture) asphalt is sufficient for stabilization. As a rule, the more open graded the material is, the lower the asphalt content required for stabilization. The asphalt used is similar to the grade normally used in that location. Use a higher viscosity (stiffer) asphalt to provide increased stability.
key_points: Target asphalt content: enough to coat/hold aggregate without filling voids, normally about 2-2.5 percent by weight of total mixture.
More open-graded material needs less asphalt for stabilization.
Use the asphalt grade normally used locally; a stiffer (higher-viscosity) asphalt increases stability.
sections.applicability: Applies when proportioning the asphalt content for a stabilized open graded drainage layer.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Covers OGM drainage-layer placement: place with a paver to minimize segregation and hit design grade/thickness, typically run through an HMA plant with asphalt cement binder (liquid asphalts used if conditions warrant), and roll only enough to seat the aggregate in place.
sections.body: Place a stabilized OGM with a paver to minimize segregation and achieve the design grade and thickness. Usually asphalt cement is used as the binder and the OGM is run through a HMA plant to achieve required coating and to allow for placement. Liquid asphalts (emulsions or cutbacks) are used if conditions warrant. An OGM requires rolling the mixture only to seat the aggregate in place.
key_points: Place with a paver to minimize segregation and achieve design grade/thickness.
Typically run through an HMA plant with asphalt cement binder; liquid asphalts used if conditions warrant.
Roll only enough to seat the aggregate -- not full densification compaction.
sections.applicability: Applies to the construction/placement of an asphalt-stabilized OGM drainage layer.
